title: Why the same program is fast on small data and slow on large
objective: By the end of this lesson you can measure the memory hierarchy on your own machine, name the two kinds of locality, and explain why hardware bets on both.

blocks.text: The load-use lesson measured a dependent walk over a 32 KB buffer at 1.87 ns per access. Run exactly the same code over a larger buffer and the number changes dramatically — not because the code changed, but because of where the data now lives.

One caveat, and the DRAM lesson later measures it: a chain is only serialised while the hardware cannot guess where it goes next. A chain whose links happen to run straight through memory in order is predictable, and modern processors work the addresses out ahead of the loads — which is why the sequential chain in that lesson comes in at 0.52 ns per access, below this machine's own L1 latency. Shuffling the chain, as here, is what removes that escape route and leaves you measuring the memory system.

Follow a randomly ordered chain of pointers through a working set, doubling the working set each time. Because each access depends on the previous one, no overlapping can hide the wait — the time per access is the memory system's honest latency for that working set size.

blocks.caption: Measured on an Apple M4
lines: working set      ns per dependent access

blocks.title: That is not a curve, it is a staircase
blocks.text: Six sizes in a row cost exactly the same, then the cost quadruples in a single doubling. A gradual curve would suggest memory gets slowly worse with size. It does not: there are distinct levels of storage, each with its own capacity and its own speed, and the steps are where the working set stopped fitting in one and fell into the next.
Reading the steps against what the machine reports

blocks.caption: The hardware's own description of itself
lines: The flat region ends at 128 KB.   The reported L1 is 128 KB.
The second climb starts at 16 MB. The reported L2 is 16 MB.

blocks.text: The measurement and the hardware's self-report agree without either having been used to produce the other. That agreement is what makes the measurement trustworthy: a number that matches an independent source is evidence, while a number that merely looks reasonable is not.

headers: The hardware feature that takes the bet
rows: Something used now will be used again soon
Keeping it in the cache after use
Something near what was used will be used soon
Fetching a whole block, not one byte

blocks.text: Both are bets about typical programs, not laws. A loop over an array rewards spatial locality; a loop counter or a frequently-called function rewards temporal locality. A program that reads memory in genuinely random order and never revisits anything defeats both, and its performance lands at the bottom step of that staircase.
The spatial bet is visible on its own. Touch a fixed number of bytes spread over a large buffer, varying only how far apart they are.

blocks.caption: Measured on the same machine
lines: touching 1,000,000 bytes spread over a 64 MB buffer at a fixed stride
128 B         6.52     <- the cost jumps here and stays
/* Below 128 bytes, several touched bytes share one fetched block, so the
fetch cost is split between them. At 128 bytes and beyond, each touch
pays for its own block. The machine reports hw.cachelinesize = 128. */

blocks.text: Constant up to 64 bytes, then a jump at 128 that persists no matter how much further apart the touches get. That is the block size, measured. Below it, several touched bytes arrive in one fetch and share its cost; at and above it, every touch pays for a full block of which it uses a fraction.

blocks.title: You are always paying for a whole block
blocks.text: Reading one byte from memory does not fetch one byte. On this machine it fetches 128. If your program uses 4 of those bytes and moves 128 bytes away, it paid for 128 and used 4 — a 3% return on the transfer. This single fact, more than any other, is what separates fast data layouts from slow ones, and the capstone at the end of this module is built on it.
What this changes about how you read your own code

items: The cost of an access is not a property of the access; it is a property of the working set
Reducing memory used can speed up code that does exactly the same work
A structure whose fields you never read still costs you, because it occupies blocks
An algorithm with more operations can beat one with fewer if its accesses are contiguous
'Optimising' by adding a lookup table can lose if the table pushes the working set to the next step

blocks.text: The fourth item is worth pausing on, because it contradicts the way algorithms are usually compared. Counting operations assumes every operation costs the same. On the staircase above, one access can cost 87 times another. An operation count is a useful first approximation and a poor final answer.

blocks.title: Build the staircase for your machine
steps: Allocate a buffer, fill it with a randomly shuffled pointer chain, and follow it
Time it for working sets from 4 KB to at least 128 MB, doubling each time
Plot or tabulate nanoseconds per access against working-set size
Identify the flat regions and the steps between them
Compare your steps with what your machine reports: sysctl -a | grep cache   (or lscpu)
Repeat with a sequential chain instead of a shuffled one and explain the difference
Now measure the stride sweep and find your block size
State your machine's cache sizes and line size, each supported by one of your own numbers
blocks.expected: Flat regions matching your cache sizes and a step at your line size, agreeing with what the system reports. The sequential version will be much faster at large sizes — that is the hardware prefetcher noticing a pattern and fetching ahead, which is why the shuffled chain is the honest way to measure latency.

cheatsheet: Memory is a staircase of levels, not a smooth curve of cost against size
A dependent pointer chase measures true latency because nothing can overlap it
Measured on an Apple M4: 1.92 ns flat to 128 KB, 7.61 ns at 256 KB, 167 ns at 128 MB
Those steps match the reported L1 of 128 KB and L2 of 16 MB
Temporal locality: reuse the same data soon. Spatial locality: use nearby data soon
Caches keep data after use (temporal) and fetch whole blocks (spatial)
Stride sweep found the jump at 128 bytes, matching hw.cachelinesize = 128
Every access pays for a whole block whether or not you use the rest of it
Operation counting assumes all operations cost the same; here one can cost 87 times another
A shuffled chain measures latency; a sequential one measures the prefetcher

checkpoint.prompt: Why does a dependent pointer chase measure memory latency more honestly than a loop over an array?

choices.B: Each access cannot begin until the previous one returns, so nothing overlaps and the wait cannot be hidden

checkpoint.explanation: An array walk lets the processor run far ahead and prefetch, which measures throughput. The chain forces one access at a time, which is what latency means.

checkpoint.prompt: The measurement was flat at 1.92 ns from 4 KB to 128 KB and then jumped to 7.61 ns at 256 KB. What does the flat region mean?

choices.A: The measurement was not sensitive enough
choices.B: Every working set in that range fit entirely in one level of cache, so every access hit at the same speed
choices.D: Small buffers are faster to allocate

checkpoint.explanation: The cost is flat while the data fits and steps when it stops fitting. The last flat size, 128 KB, matches the L1 the machine reports.

checkpoint.prompt: A stride sweep showed a constant cost up to 64 bytes and a jump at 128. What has been measured?

choices.B: The cache line size: below it several touches share one fetched block, at and above it each touch pays for its own

checkpoint.explanation: The system reports hw.cachelinesize = 128, matching the measurement made without consulting it.

checkpoint.prompt: Why can an algorithm performing more operations beat one performing fewer?

choices.B: Operation counting assumes every operation costs the same, but a memory access can cost tens of times another depending on where the data sits
choices.D: Only when the data is sorted

checkpoint.explanation: On the staircase measured here the ratio between the cheapest and most expensive access was about 87. An operation count cannot see that.
